note.question: Can a fully decentralized two-sided search market generate persistent inequality between ex ante identical groups, and do cheaper search or side payments reliably reduce that inequality?
note.overview: Agents on two sides repeatedly pay to meet and simultaneously decide whether to accept one another. Each side's optimal reservation threshold depends on the other side's acceptance behavior, and the paper derives and stability-refines Bayesian Nash equilibria that may endogenously break symmetry.

models.method: The paper derives stationary reservation-rule best responses for each population, solves their intersections under Pareto payoffs, applies local stability as an equilibrium-selection criterion, conducts search-cost and welfare comparative statics, generalizes through a mean-excess condition, and constructs extensions with asymmetric fundamentals and monetary offers.

sources.quote: To summarize the previous example, when monetary transfers are not allowed, the maximal equilibrium inequality is for one population to have the expected payoff of 11.9, whereas the other has the expected payoff of 15.5; when mon­ etary transfers are allowed, the disadvantaged population may be the only one making monetary transfers, and its net expected payoff can be 11.6, whereas the advantaged popula­ tion’s net payoff becomes 17.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: An unmatched agent pays a per-meeting search cost to meet a random member of the other population. At the meeting, each participant privately observes the payoff that the match would give that participant and simultaneously accepts or rejects. A match forms only if both accept; otherwise both remain unmatched and may pay to search again. Stationary reservation thresholds are mutually consistent in Bayesian Nash equilibrium.
